name: Signed agent requests (Web Bot Auth)
plain: An agent can sign its web requests so a site can check who sent them.
meaning: Web Bot Auth uses HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421). The agent adds Signature, Signature-Input and a Signature-Agent header that points to a public key directory. The site fetches the keys and verifies the signature, so a user agent name cannot be faked. Google lists it as experimental for its own agent, and cloud agent platforms are adding it.

web.api: Signature, Signature-Input and Signature-Agent request headers; key directory at /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory

steps: Agent signs selected request parts with a private key
Agent sends Signature, Signature-Input and Signature-Agent
Site fetches the public key directory
Site verifies the signature and trusts or denies the agent

chrome.note: Sent by agent platforms, not by the browser

fields.name: Signature
fields.range: signature bytes for chosen request parts

fields.name: Signature-Input
fields.range: which parts were signed, created time, key id, tag

fields.name: Signature-Agent
fields.range: URL of the agent's key directory

limits.headline: Can prove which agent operator made a request
limits.user_action: Nothing for people. The agent platform signs for you
can: Check a cryptographic signature on a request
Look up the operator's published keys
Allow known agents and rate limit the rest
cannot: Tell you what the agent will do
Work for agents that do not sign
Prove a person approved the action
limits.reach_label: A signed header set per request
limits.differs: Support is new and uneven. Sites must choose to honor it. A signature proves the operator, not the task or the person behind it.

story.what_it_is: A signed envelope on each request. The site checks the signature the way a shop checks a stamp.

marketing.name: HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421)
marketing.pitch: Standard for signing parts of HTTP messages.

marketing.name: Web Bot Auth
marketing.pitch: Docs describe how verified bots sign requests.

story.for_you: You never see it. If you use an agent, the platform may sign its requests so sites can recognize it and treat it well.
story.for_makers: Verify signatures against the published directory and check created and expires times. Use it for an allow list, not as proof of a safe request. Keep a fallback for unsigned agents.

use_cases.example: A site allows signed requests from a known agent and challenges the rest.
A retailer lets a verified shopping agent read stock without a challenge.
A publisher lets a signed AI fetcher read pages under its terms.
An agent team signs requests so partner sites can recognize them.
An internal API accepts only signed agent calls.
A booking site gives signed agents a calmer rate limit.

technical_bounds: Standards still in draft at the IETF
